entries.seminar_title: The Market for Antibiotics: Sorting, Signals, and Regulation in Kenya
entries.speaker: Michael Dinerstein
entries.abstract: Antibiotic use creates a resistance externality, but imperfect information and misaligned incentives complicate regulation. We study retail health markets in western Kenya, where patients choose between pharmacies and clinics and can request drugs directly. We combine evidence from a market census, patient and provider surveys, clinical vignettes, and randomized standardized-patient experiments in an equilibrium model of patient sorting, diagnostic effort, pricing, and dispensing. Roughly one-third of surveyed patients receive incorrect antibiotic treatment. The estimated model indicates that overtreatment is primarily driven by incentives: some patients value antibiotics beyond their expected clinical benefit, and providers respond to dispensing profits and incentives to attract customers. Undertreatment primarily reflects incomplete information. Most patients with bacterial infections have low perceived antibiotic need. Many of these patients choose pharmacies, where limited diagnostic effort leaves some infections unidentified. We evaluate policy counterfactuals in equilibrium, allowing patients to adjust provider choice and drug requests and providers to adjust diagnostic effort, dispensing rules, and prices. Restricting pharmacy antibiotic sales and taxing antibiotics reduce overtreatment but also substantially increase undertreatment. Removing providers’ financial motives and incentives to attract customers reduces both over- and undertreatment at clinics, which already acquire diagnostic information. At pharmacies, it reduces overtreatment but increases undertreatment.

entries.seminar_title: Teaching Practices, Behavioral Change, and Socio-Emotional Skill Formation
entries.speaker: Laia Navarro-Sola
entries.abstract: Schools shape skills that matter beyond academic achievement. Teachers are central to this process, yet whether these effects arise from fixed teacher attributes or from malleable instructional practices remains unclear. We investigate this question through a randomized intervention in Spanish secondary schools. The program equips treated teachers with tools to observe students' socio-emotional skills and provide structured feedback during routine instruction, thus generating exogenous variation in instructional practices. We combine external observations of student behavior with independent measures of teaching practices, survey measures of socio-emotional skills, and administrative records of grades and absences. The intervention improves students' socio-emotional behaviors in an externally assessed group activity and increases academic achievement, with particularly pronounced academic gains among students with lower baseline performance. These improvements translate into a substantial reduction in the probability of failing at least one subject. In contrast, we find no average improvement in socio-emotional behaviors observed during regular classroom instruction, although there is suggestive evidence of larger behavioral gains among students with weaker baseline socio-emotional skills and those from disadvantaged backgrounds. We also find evidence of changes in classroom interactions and instructional practices, which may contribute to the observed academic improvements. Together, these findings indicate that malleable teaching practices can improve academic outcomes and the expression of socio-emotional competencies, while highlighting that behavioral responses depend on the context in which they are measured, as well as students' initial characteristics.
